title: Automatic Reference Counting
subtitle: How Swift knows when an object is no longer needed — and why it can be wrong.

sections.body:
Every class instance in Swift carries a count of how many strong references point at it. Create a reference, the count goes up. Let one go out of scope or reassign it, the count goes down. When the count hits zero, the object is deallocated immediately — `deinit` runs, and the memory is freed.

This is ARC, and "automatic" means the compiler inserts the counting for you, not that it thinks about ownership on your behalf. It's not a garbage collector: there's no background sweep, no pause, and no detection of unreachable islands. The rule is purely local — count reached zero, free it.

That immediacy is a real advantage, and the missing island detection is the one hole you have to cover yourself.

Think of a shared apartment and its keys.

Every person holding a key is a strong reference. While at least one key is out there, the landlord can't re-let the flat — someone might walk in. When the last key is handed back, the flat is cleared out that same moment.

Nobody counts *rooms*, and nobody checks whether the keyholders are actually still using the place. Two flatmates who've each got a key to the other's flat and never leave will keep both flats occupied forever. That's a retain cycle, and no amount of counting keys will notice it.

sections.caption: `deinit` runs the instant the last strong reference disappears — not later.

sections.title: Reference counting in action
sections.altText: Two variables hold strong references to a Person object, giving it a retain count of two. As each variable goes out of scope the count drops, and at zero the object is deallocated.

steps.caption: Creating the instance takes the count to 1.
Assigning to another variable takes it to 2.
Both references go out of scope. Count hits 0, deinit runs immediately.

sections.body:
The compiler emits `swift_retain` and `swift_release` calls around reference assignments, and the count lives in the object's header next to its type metadata.

Three details worth knowing:

**The optimiser removes most of them.** ARC traffic you'd expect from reading the source is largely elided when the compiler can prove a reference outlives its uses. What's left is usually at ownership boundaries.

**There are two counts.** A strong count and an unowned count. When the strong count hits zero the object is deinitialised and its stored properties released, but the memory isn't returned while unowned references still exist — it becomes a zombie whose slot is reserved so that touching it can trap deterministically rather than reading someone else's data.

**`weak` costs more than `strong`.** Weak references go through a side table so they can all be zeroed when the object dies. Reading a weak reference is not free, which is why `unowned` exists as the cheaper option for cases where you can guarantee the lifetime.

sections.title: Expecting ARC to clean up a cycle
sections.body:
ARC frees an object when its count reaches zero, and nothing more. Two objects holding strong references to each other keep each other's counts at one forever, even after every outside reference is gone. They're unreachable, they're leaked, and no background process will ever come and collect them.

Breaking cycles is your job, using `weak` or `unowned` on one side of the relationship.
ARC frees an object the moment its strong count hits zero — deterministically, with no collector. It cannot see cycles, so every strong reference you create is a lifetime decision you own.

title: Weak vs Unowned
subtitle: Two ways to reference something without keeping it alive — and the crash that separates them.

sections.body:
Both `weak` and `unowned` reference an object without increasing its strong count, so neither keeps the object alive. The difference is entirely about what happens when the object dies first.

A `weak` reference is automatically set to `nil` at that moment. It must therefore be declared `var` and optional, and you check it before use.

An `unowned` reference is not zeroed. It keeps pointing where the object used to be. Using it after the object is gone traps and terminates the process.

So the choice isn't safety versus speed. It's a statement about lifetime: `unowned` means "I guarantee this outlives me", and the crash is what happens when your guarantee turns out to be wrong.

`weak` is a contact in your phone. If they change their number, your entry updates to "no longer available". You check before dialling, and nothing bad happens if they've gone.

`unowned` is a street address you memorised. If they move out, the address doesn't update — it still points at a building. Turning up expecting them is the crash: you were certain they'd be there, and they weren't.

sections.caption: `unowned` fits a genuine lifetime guarantee; `weak` fits anything less certain.

sections.title: What happens when the object dies
sections.altText: A weak reference becomes nil when its target is deallocated. An unowned reference keeps pointing at freed memory and traps if used.

steps.caption: Neither reference contributes to the strong count, so the object can die.
The weak reference is zeroed automatically — you check it and move on.
The unowned reference is left dangling. Touching it terminates the process.

sections.body:
Zeroing isn't free. Every `weak` reference to an object is registered in a side table keyed by that object, so when it deallocates the runtime can walk the table and nil them all. That's an extra allocation for the table and a lock around access, and reading a weak reference means loading through it and retaining the result so it can't die mid-expression.

`unowned` skips the side table. Instead the object keeps a separate *unowned count*, and while that count is above zero the memory isn't returned to the allocator even after `deinit` has run — the object becomes a zombie holding its own slot. That's what makes the failure a clean deterministic trap rather than a read of whatever was allocated there next.

`unowned(unsafe)` drops even that, giving you a raw dangling pointer with undefined behaviour on access. It exists for interop and hot paths; it should be rare.

sections.title: Choosing unowned to avoid the optional
sections.body:
The `if let` isn't the cost you think it is, and the crash is worse than you think. `unowned` is right when the lifetime relationship is structural — a child that is created by its parent, stored only by its parent, and cannot possibly be reached after the parent is gone.

It's wrong the moment the other object's lifetime is controlled by something outside your type: a view controller in a navigation stack, a cell being recycled, a network callback, anything the system may tear down on its own schedule. When in doubt, `weak`.
`weak` becomes nil when the object dies; `unowned` becomes a trap. Pick `unowned` only when you can state the invariant that makes the object's longer life certain.

title: Retain Cycles
subtitle: When two objects keep each other alive and ARC can never free either.

sections.body:
A retain cycle is a loop of strong references. A holds B strongly, B holds A strongly, and each keeps the other's count at one. Every outside reference can disappear and both counts still sit above zero, so ARC never frees either. Nothing is reachable and nothing is released.

That's a leak, and on iOS it's usually invisible: no crash, no error, just memory that grows a bit every time the user visits a screen. You find it when the app is killed for memory pressure after twenty minutes of use, or you don't find it at all.

Cycles need at least two participants, but they don't need exactly two. Three-object loops and closure-shaped loops are just as common.

Two people are holding a door open for each other.

Neither will go through until the other does, and neither will leave. Everyone else has gone home. From outside the building nothing is happening and nobody can reach them, but the door is still occupied and always will be.

Someone has to be willing to walk away first. That's what making one reference `weak` does: it says this side isn't going to insist.

sections.caption: Ownership should point one way. The back-reference is the one to weaken.

sections.title: A retain cycle
sections.altText: A Parent object holds a strong reference to a Child, and the Child holds a strong reference back to the Parent. With the external reference gone, both counts remain at one and neither is freed.

steps.caption: Both objects reference each other strongly.
The last outside reference is released.
Each still holds the other at a count of one. Nothing reaches zero, so nothing is freed.

sections.heading: The four shapes
sections.body:
**Where they actually come from**

In practice almost every cycle in an iOS codebase is one of four shapes:

1. **A child holding its parent strongly** — the example above. Fix: `weak var parent`.
2. **A strong delegate** — the delegating object holds its delegate, which is usually its owner. Fix: `weak var delegate`, which is why the convention exists.
3. **A closure stored on `self` that captures `self`** — the object owns the closure, the closure owns the object. Fix: `[weak self]` in the capture list.
4. **A long-lived observer or subscription that captures `self`** — a Combine `AnyCancellable`, a timer target, a notification block. The subscription outlives the screen and drags it along.

Recognising the shape is faster than reasoning from first principles each time.

sections.title: Assuming no crash means no leak
sections.body:
A retain cycle produces no error, no warning and no crash at the point it's created. The symptom is a memory graph that grows, and the eventual jetsam kill looks nothing like the code that caused it.

The cheapest defence is a `deinit` with a log on your screens and view models during development. Push and pop the screen; if the log doesn't fire, you have a cycle, and you know exactly which type to look at.
A cycle is a loop of strong references that ARC can't see out of. Decide which object owns which, make ownership point one way, and weaken the reference pointing back.

title: Closure Capture
subtitle: Capture lists, and deciding what a stored closure should keep alive.

sections.body:
When a closure mentions a variable from its surrounding scope, it captures it — and if that variable is a class reference, the capture is strong by default. The object stays alive for as long as the closure does.

A capture list, the `[...]` before the parameters, changes that. `[weak self]` captures `self` weakly, making it optional inside. `[unowned self]` captures it without a strong reference and without zeroing. You can also capture a snapshot: `[value]` copies the current value rather than referring to the variable.

The decision is always the same question: should this closure keep this object alive until it runs?

A capture list is the fine print on a standing order.

By default: "pay Sam £10 a month, and Sam must remain a customer for this to make sense" — the order keeps the account open.

`[weak self]`: "pay Sam £10 a month if Sam still has an account; if not, skip it." The order no longer forces the account to stay open, and it quietly does nothing once Sam has gone.

That last clause is the part people forget. Weak capture doesn't just avoid a leak, it changes the behaviour when the object is gone — from "this runs" to "this silently doesn't".

sections.caption: Capturing a value instead of `self` sidesteps the lifetime question entirely.

sections.title: A closure cycle and how a capture list breaks it
sections.altText: A Downloader holds a closure in a stored property, and the closure strongly captures the Downloader, forming a loop. A weak capture replaces that back-edge so the loop is broken.

steps.caption: The object stores the closure, and the closure captures the object. That's the loop.
Neither count can reach zero, so both leak.
A weak capture removes the back-edge. The object can now be freed, and the closure's `self` simply becomes nil.

sections.body:
A capture list is evaluated *when the closure is created*, not when it runs. `[weak self]` takes a weak reference at creation; `[value]` copies whatever `value` holds at that instant, and later changes to the variable don't affect the captured copy.

This is why `[value]` is a genuine third option rather than a curiosity: it converts a reference-to-storage capture into a snapshot, which is often what you actually wanted and removes the lifetime question completely.

`guard let self else { return }` works because Swift 5.8 allows shadowing `self` in a guard. It promotes the weak reference to a strong one for the body's duration, so `self` can't be deallocated halfway through — without it, each separate `self?.` could see a different answer as another thread releases the last reference between them.

sections.title: Treating `[weak self]` as free insurance
sections.body:
A weakly captured `self` that has been deallocated makes the closure body a no-op. If that body was saving a draft, releasing a lock, completing a continuation, or calling a completion handler someone is awaiting, the work silently doesn't happen — and there's no crash and no log to find it by.

For one-shot work that must finish, capture strongly on purpose and let the object live until the work is done. `[weak self]` is for closures whose lifetime `self` owns, not for every closure.

Capture lists are evaluated at closure creation and decide what the closure keeps alive. Weak when `self` owns the closure; strong when the work must complete; a value snapshot when you never needed the object at all.
